messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: The DOI and URL exactly match the citation text provided for the Masters et al. 2025 article (10.1016/j.seppur.2025.134308).

The cited text explicitly describes methanol extractions to estimate accumulation of PFAS on treatment materials and discusses PFAS sorption/adsorption to the filter, membrane, IX resin, and greensand (e.g., “PFAS extractions… revealed accumulation of PFAS” and “PFAS sorption to treatment materials”). This corresponds to a sorption endpoint.

E01 and E04 state that methanol extractions were performed to estimate accumulation of PFAS on treatment materials, that the highest solid phase PFAS concentrations were in the 0.2 µm filter replicates per gram of material, that membrane sections and IX softening resin had ~10× lower concentrations, and that greensand had the lowest concentrations. E01 and E05 indicate PFOS contributed 60–85% of total PFAS mass or solid-phase concentration. E02 and E04 state that long-chain PFAS preferentially adsorbed to the 0.2 µm filter and membrane, and that sorption to greensand was more influenced by functional group than chain length. These statements collectively support the interpretation provided.

The source repeatedly refers to “PFAS sorption to treatment materials,” “adsorbed” PFOS, and “accumulation of PFAS on treatment materials” (E01, E04, E05), aligning with the summarized reported term of PFAS adsorption/accumulation on treatment materials.

E01 and E05 describe methanol extractions on pretreatment materials and one BW30 RO element to estimate PFAS accumulation. No kinetic data or varied operating-condition extractions are reported in the supplied text. Inferring that accumulation was only evaluated via methanol extraction of select materials and that kinetics or absolute sorbed masses under varying conditions were not characterized in the provided text is a reasonable design-based inference.

E04 and E08 identify the treated water as AFFF-impacted groundwater. E04 mentions evaluation of PFAS sorption to pretreatment materials and one BW30 element in a closed-circuit membrane system, and E01/E05 refer to 0.2 µm filter, IX softening resin, and greensand filter media. Together these support the described matrix as AFFF-impacted groundwater fed to a CCMS with those pretreatment materials and a BW30 RO element.

E04 describes experiments conducted using a closed-circuit membrane system, and E06 refers to the “CCMS feed” and a “recirculation experiment.” However, the text does not explicitly state that PFAS extraction from solids occurred specifically after a recirculation experiment, though that is plausible. The CCMS with pretreatment and RO is supported, but the timing qualifier about a recirculation experiment prior to extraction is only inferred.
The field correctly leaves unit as null for a categorical description of system type; no numeric unit applies.

E04 and E08 clearly state that the treated water is AFFF-impacted groundwater. E01 and E05 indicate PFOS was measured at the highest concentration in the groundwater and that PFOS represented 60–85% of solid phase PFAS, consistent with describing the groundwater as having high PFOS concentration and a mixture of PFAS.
This is a descriptive water type; leaving unit null is appropriate.

E03 lists the general water quality analyses performed: dissolved iron, hardness, conductivity, pH, TOC, major anions, and major cations, matching the statement that these parameters were measured. The note that specific values are not reported in the supplied text correctly reflects the provided excerpts.
This is a description of measured parameters, not a numeric condition; unit is appropriately null.

E01 and E05 state that PFOS was the dominant PFAS adsorbed on all media, contributing 60–85% of total PFAS mass or solid phase concentration, and that PFOS was measured at the highest concentration in the groundwater (approximately a third of total quantified PFAS). This supports PFOS as the dominant PFAS in both groundwater and sorbed phases.

E06 and E02 describe multiple PFAS classes and specific examples (e.g., PFBS, PFPeA, FBSA, FPeSA, 10:2 FTS, 10:2 fluorotelomer carboxylic acids, perfluorododecanoic acid, perfluorotridecanoic acid, perfluorodecane sulfonate), which are long- and short-chain PFSAs, PFCAs, FTSs, and FASAs in AFFF-impacted groundwater. This aligns with the summarized mixture description.

E01 notes that solid phase concentrations were significantly lower (~10 times) for membrane sections and IX softening resin compared to the 0.2 µm filter, and E05 states the 0.2 µm filter had approximately 10× greater solid phase concentration than any other material. The approximate numeric value of ~10 (fold higher) is directly supported.
The source uses a relative description (“approximately 10x greater solid phase concentration”). Using “fold higher” as the unit for the relative factor is consistent with the text.

E01 and E05 support that the 0.2 µm cartridge filter had approximately 10× greater solid phase PFAS concentration per gram of material than other extracted materials (membrane sections, IX softening resin, greensand).

E01 states PFOS was the dominant PFAS adsorbed, contributing between 60–85% of total PFAS mass, and E05 notes PFOS represented 60–85% of total solid phase concentration depending on material. The range 60–85 is correctly captured.
The text expresses this as a percent contribution to total PFAS mass/solid phase concentration. The unit “% of total extracted PFAS mass” correctly represents this.
The qualifiers restate that PFOS was dominant on all media and contributed 60–85% of total PFAS mass, which is directly supported by E01 and E05.

The study reports relative accumulation (e.g., ~10× higher concentration in the 0.2 µm filter, PFOS fraction) and qualitative trends in chain length and functional group effects (E01, E02, E04, E05) without providing isotherms or breakthrough curves for these materials. Characterizing this as descriptive_only for adsorption-medium comparison follows from the nature of the reported data.

E01, E02, E04, and E05 show that the study reports relative PFAS accumulation and compositional shifts on several materials in a pilot membrane system, rather than detailed equilibrium adsorption metrics. Inferring that this limits direct quantitative comparison to conventional adsorbent selection data is a reasonable analyst judgment based on those fields.

The cited excerpts (E01, E04, E05, E06) only discuss extraction and accumulation of parent PFAS species on treatment materials. There is no mention of transformation products or defluorination, so inferring that observations relate to phase transfer (sorption) rather than degradation is consistent with the provided text.

The article title and E04 specify a pilot-scale investigation using a closed-circuit membrane system treating AFFF-impacted groundwater. E01 and E05 describe methanol extraction of PFAS from pretreatment materials and one BW30 element (0.2 µm filter, IX softening resin, greensand). This supports the summarized pilot-scale study description.
The work is an experimental pilot-scale investigation reporting new PFAS rejection and sorption data, fitting the classification as a primary experiment.

E01, E04, and E05 describe PFAS sorption/accumulation on a 0.2 µm cartridge filter, BW30 RO membrane, IX softening resin, and greensand media, and that methanol extractions were used to quantify accumulated PFAS. This matches the stated treatment description focused on sorption to these materials and subsequent methanol extraction.

result.record_usable_rationale: Core elements—source identity, matrix, treatment materials, sorption endpoint, and quantitative findings on relative accumulation and PFOS fraction—are correctly extracted and directly supported by the cited text. One operating-condition detail (timing relative to recirculation) is partially supported but does not affect interpretation of the main adsorption evidence, so the record remains suitable for synthesis with minor caution about that qualifier.
